intuition.text: Look at one thing and try to answer two different questions about it. The details you need can change even while the thing in front of you stays exactly the same. That is the idea behind levels of description.
intuition.situation: The public DotLn kit guide describes how a planning pass sequences orders, a gate records a result and a hook can block a write. Our four entries describe one afternoon at different scales. They are separate sources. You have to open the plan to find the reason for doing the guide first. The letters in the check result alone cannot tell you that reason.

example.name: What can one observation tell you?
example.description:
Imagine a tutorial that links to a setup guide. During a 45-minute work session your team revises the guide first. A guard blocks one extra edit while a checker follows the saved guide’s links. Here are four invented entries you could lay side by side after that afternoon. The labels name types of DotLn records.

Hook refusal · “Edit blocked.” The guard attached the refusal to the “Guide links” run.

Gate row · “Guide links passed.” The checker recorded its verdict for the “Guide revision” assignment. The refusal and the pass share the “Guide links” run.

Work order · “Revise setup steps and check links.” The “Guide revision” assignment belongs to the “Tutorial release” plan. The passing check supplies evidence for the second requirement.

Planning pass · “Guide first, tutorial next.” The author of the “Tutorial release” plan put the two jobs in that order because tomorrow’s tutorial links to the guide.

step0.title: Read the hook refusal
step0.text: In the 45-minute recording, find the “Edit blocked” entry for the setup guide. It names the Guide links run in which the guard refused that extra write.

step1.title: Find the gate row
step1.text: Read the “Guide links passed” row with the same run identifier. It records the saved guide that was checked. The refusal and the pass answer different questions about that run.

step2.title: Read the work order
step2.text: Follow the row’s work-order identifier to the existing assignment, “Revise setup steps and check links.” Its first requirement needs separate evidence.

step3.title: Read the planning pass
step3.text: Read the planning pass named by that assignment. Its written ordering, “Guide first, tutorial next,” gives you the dependency. Grouping results cannot supply the planner’s reason.

item1.relevance: Read an operation as a trace, a span or an event.
item1.explanation: A trace's root span typically represents the whole operation and its child spans can represent parts of it. A span can also hold named, timestamped events. For an HTTP request, a child span might time the database query while a span event could mark a brief occurrence during the query.

limits.item0: A gate row can seal off the hook's detail while you ask whether the checked version passed. If an edit slips through and changes the guide, use the event trail and the gate's recorded revision to find out which version the pass covers.
limits.item1: The analogy uses run, order and pass identifiers to join the views. A gate covering several orders may supply evidence to each of them. The order's criterion and the planning pass's reason for adding the guide still live in their written records.
limits.item2: The stream example assumes the recording ends. With a live feed, each group needs a closing rule before an array of its events can appear.

steps.refusal: Did the extra edit get saved? The guard blocked it while the checker was reading the guide. The refusal records that one attempted change.
steps.result: Did the links work? The checker followed them in the saved copy and recorded a pass. The blocked edit and the passing check happened during the same run.
steps.promise: What did the team agree to deliver? The assignment called for revised setup steps and working links. The passing row answers only the part about links.
steps.dependency: Why do the guide first? The tutorial will send readers there tomorrow. The plan records that dependency. To find out what happened to one edit, you must look back down at the refusal.

model.caption: Read from the bottom up. The bottom arrow joins two records from the same check. The next arrow links that check to the assignment it helps verify. The top arrow leads to the plan that scheduled the work.

specimen.title: Read one line of test output
specimen.source: We made a tiny guide for this test. It contains two links, #install and #start, and headings named install and start. We ran the check and the runner printed this line.
specimen.reading: Look for the small word “ok.” It consists of two characters. Read it as a test verdict and it means the first check passed. The words after the dash came from the name we wrote for the test. They tell you exactly what was checked.
specimen.question: Would the test still pass if the setup instructions were out of date?
specimen.answer: Yes. The checker only looked for the two link targets. The same green result can sit beside an outdated paragraph. Now read the assignment below to find out what else the team promised.

intuition.text: A log line can tell you that a write was refused. A short report can tell you how often that happened across the whole check. Chunking starts by giving neighboring details a shared boundary, then lets you carry one small description per group into the report. Choose what each group keeps by asking what the report needs to answer.
intuition.situation: This is an analogy to DotLn's public README.md demo. After a refused deletion in a fixture repository, it presents a numbered timeline and a line of glyphs derived from the same event log. Our guide check takes a different event list and shows how a short line can keep a refusal visible while the individual events remain available.

example.name: A guide check in chunks
example.description: The recording has five events in order. The run opens, the guide is read, a write is refused, the links are checked and the gate passes. With the starting width of two, the first pair is open and read. The second pair is refusal and link check. The pass stands alone. The summary still counts five events and one refusal. Set the group size to {chunkSize} or change it under Try another value.

step0.title: Read the recording
step0.text: Start with Run opened, Guide read, Write refused, Links checked and Gate passed, in that order.

step1.title: Make consecutive chunks
step1.text: Start at the first unused event and add events in order up to the limit of {chunkSize}. Keep the final group even when it is short. Save each group's members and count its refused writes.

step2.title: Summarize the guide check
step2.text: Add the groups' event and refusal counts. Report those totals alongside the number of chunks so the whole check can be read at a glance.

pseudocode.ordinary:
guideEvents = [Run opened, Guide read, Write refused, Links checked, Gate passed]

chunks = []
for start in range(0, length(guideEvents), chunkSize):
    members = slice(guideEvents, start, start + chunkSize)
    chunks.append(chunk(members, count(members, Write refused)))

guideCheck = sumEventAndRefusalCounts(chunks)
guideCheck.chunkCount = length(chunks)

item0.explanation: With only a size argument, bufferCount opens the next group after a full group is emitted. When the source completes it also emits any remaining group. Mapping each emitted list to a chunk with counts makes it possible to build a report from those chunks.

intuition.text: Ask a rulebook whether you can book a room. A rulebook that proves both the booking claim and its negation for the same room and slot is inconsistent. In ordinary propositional logic, one assignment that makes every premise true is enough to show that sound rules cannot derive such a pair from those premises.
intuition.situation: DotLn’s public kit guide says that reusing a complete review pass requires the current code identity and time limits. A change to the limits calls for another run. This is an analogy for matching the subject of two claims before comparing them. Two reports that look incompatible can describe different runs, just as two booking notices can describe different slots.

example.name: Cedar Room in slot 3
example.description: A clearance for Cedar Room in slot 3 entails that the room is bookable. A hold covering that same room and slot entails that it is not bookable. Start with the clearance alone. It says nothing about the projector.

step0.title: Read the clearance
step0.text: Fix the room and time slot first. The clearance gives one conclusion about Cedar Room in slot 3. You may book it.

step1.title: Give two possible readings
step1.text: One possible schedule has Cedar Room bookable with a working projector. In another, the room is bookable with a broken projector. Each schedule separately satisfies the clearance. The rule leaves the projector question open.

step2.title: Read the hold
step2.text: Apply the hold to precisely the same room and slot. The room is now also declared unavailable under the rules. The clearance remains in force for this comparison.

step3.title: Compare the booking claims
step3.text: Both conclusions concern whether Cedar Room is bookable in slot 3. No assignment can make that claim and its negation true together. The record with both reports is inconsistent.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: follow the claims in one hand-worked room schedule.
subject ← Cedar Room in slot 3
claims ← Bookable(subject) from the clearance

witness A ← Bookable(subject) true, ProjectorWorks(Cedar Room) true
witness B ← Bookable(subject) true, ProjectorWorks(Cedar Room) false
both witnesses satisfy claims

add ¬Bookable(subject) to claims from the hold

check whether one assignment satisfies Bookable(subject) and ¬Bookable(subject)
report a contradiction for Cedar Room in slot 3

limits.item1: A few deductions without a contradiction leave consistency open. The clearance-only example has a stronger witness because a whole assignment satisfies all its premises.
limits.item2: The DotLn analogy is about matching the conditions of two reports. A recorded run covers particular checks, and the logical claim concerns every conclusion that the rules can derive.

intuition.text: A derivation settles a yes answer the moment you find it. Giving a dependable no also takes a reason why every possible derivation has been accounted for. A decision procedure always finishes with a correct yes or no about whether the requested claim follows from the rules.
intuition.situation: The DotLn kit guide describes a manifest check that hashes a finite list of compiled runtime and test files and names any that are changed or missing. This is an analogy for looking through a known set of candidates so the result has a stopping point. A time limit can stop a real check before it has reached a verdict.

example.name: Lantern relay
example.description: Dock starts lit. Each wire leads from a lit lantern to one it can light. With the extra Bell-to-Cove wire off, the search lights Dock, Steps, Bell and Beacon. Beacon is reachable. Cove has a wire pointing out toward Bell, but you cannot follow it backwards into Cove. Turn on the Bell-to-Cove wire under Try another value to change the second verdict.

step0.title: Start at Dock
step0.text: Mark Dock as lit and put it first in the queue. The wire from Bell to Cove is present when the Bell-to-Cove setting is 1.

step1.title: Follow each available rule
step1.text: For every lantern in the queue, try each outgoing wire and queue each newly lit lantern. The wire from Bell back to Steps reaches a lantern already marked. You keep that mark and leave the queue alone.

step2.title: Read the verdicts
step2.text: Each lantern can enter the queue only once, so every queued lantern eventually has its wires checked. Any derivation from Dock must follow those wires. Once the queue is exhausted, membership in the lit set answers each claim.

pseudocode.ordinary:
rules ← [Dock → Steps, Steps → Bell, Bell → Steps,
         Bell → Beacon, Cove → Bell]
if coveWire is 1, add Bell → Cove to rules
lit ← set containing Dock
queue ← [Dock]

for each source in queue, including entries added below
    for each rule source → destination in rules
        if destination is absent from lit
            add destination to lit
            append destination to queue

return [Beacon in lit, Cove in lit]

item0.relevance: Marks every vertex reachable from a source in a directed graph.
item0.explanation: Sedgewick and Wayne’s Java implementation follows outgoing edges depth-first and marks a vertex before considering its neighbors. The lantern relay explores with a queue. In both examples, testing a mark after exploration answers reachability.

item1.title: Panu Raatikainen on decidable theories
item1.supports: Sections 1.3 and 4.2 distinguish generating the members of a set from deciding membership, and define a theory’s decidability in terms of its theorems.

item2.title: DotLn kit guide on gates
item2.supports: The kit-verification task hashes the compiled runtime and test files named in its manifest. The gate reports time exhaustion separately from a check failure.

item0.why: A tree of paths can revisit Steps endlessly. The relay finishes by recording each distinct lantern just once.

item1.why: The lit set is a membership question with a stopping rule for both answers.

item2.why: A truth table uses a different finite search and gives a verdict after all relevant assignments have been considered.

limits.item0: The stop argument relies on the fixed set of lanterns and the rule that each mark is permanent. A system with rules that can keep creating new claims needs its own reason to stop.
limits.item1: Even a finite search can be costly. A model with many interacting parts may have a large set of states to check.
limits.item2: A no answers the claim under the given wires. An unmodeled source of light could change the real scene. In the DotLn analogy, an interrupted check can leave a file unjudged.

intuition.text: When two representations are reversible, ask whether they also preserve the operations you care about. If you can join two words and then encode them, or encode the words and then join their codes, an isomorphism makes the two routes agree for every pair. Each word must also have exactly one counterpart in the chosen set of codes, with a unique way back.
intuition.situation: Consider a catalog export as an analogy. DotLn-Angular’s public Toolbox catalog document says a resolved relation carries the exact ID of its target. When reviewing an export, match entries by ID. Following a link and then looking up the exported target should take you to the same entry as looking up the exported source and then following its link.

example.name: Join L and R in two representations
example.description: Follow the same pair, L and R, along both paths. Write their digits 1 and 2 together in base three and their value is 1 × 3 + 2 = 5. Encode the letters separately and combine the two codes by shifting and adding, and you also get 5. The last step tests the fixed candidate 3. Open Gödel numbering to run the encoder and try other candidate numbers.

step0.title: Join the words first
step0.text: Put the letters of R after L to get LR. To encode it, read the symbol digits in order as a base-three numeral.

step1.title: Join the codes first
step1.text: Encode L and R separately. Shift the prefix code left one base-three place for each letter in the suffix, then add the suffix code. R takes one place. An empty suffix takes zero places even though its code is written 0. The shift reserves exactly the space that the suffix fills.

step2.title: Go back to the word
step2.text: Read the joined code’s base-three digits in order and turn each into its letter. The letters return as LR. The empty word has code zero. Joining with the empty word changes neither the word nor the code.

step3.title: Find the image
step3.text: The matching set on the code side is called the image. It contains zero and the positive numbers whose base-three digits are all 1 or 2. Each such numeral spells exactly one word. The candidate contains a zero digit in its positive numeral, so it falls outside that set.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: this pair of words gives both routes through the diagram.
joinedWord = concatenate(leftWord, rightWord)  // L then R gives LR
fromWords = encode(joinedWord)

leftCode = encode(leftWord)
rightCode = encode(rightWord)
places = length of rightCode in base three (zero places for the empty word)
fromCodes = leftCode × 3^places + rightCode
check fromWords = fromCodes

recovered = decode(fromCodes)
check recovered = joinedWord  // LR
check encode(empty word) = 0

image = zero and the positive integers with only digits 1 and 2 in base three
check probeCode is outside image  // the candidate has a zero digit

item0.relevance: A textbook treatment of the operation of joining words.
item0.explanation: Al Doerr and Ken Levasseur show how pairing the letters of two equal-sized alphabets gives a pairing of all their strings. Translating letter by letter preserves the whole string’s order and makes concatenation agree on both sides. Our example also gives the translated digits a place value.

item0.title: Gödel, Escher, Bach — Basic Books
item0.supports: Identifies Hofstadter’s book and describes its treatment of self-reference across mathematical, musical and visual forms.

item1.title: Applied Discrete Structures §14.2 — Free Monoids and Languages
item1.supports: Defines concatenation, identifies the empty word as its identity and shows how a bijection of alphabets extends to an isomorphism of their strings.

item2.title: DotLn-Angular — Toolbox catalog, Data and provenance
item2.supports: Documents exact target IDs for resolved relations and explains the titles retained as unlinked text.

item0.why: Run this same encoding and arithmetic join, then decode the result and try a number outside the image.

item1.why: An interpretation assigns a reading to symbols. In an isomorphism, the specified operations must agree on their corresponding inputs as well.

item2.why: The arithmetic join is a small example of expressing a rule about written strings as an operation on their numbers.

limits.item0: The arithmetic operation here is shift and add. Ordinary addition can produce a number outside the image, and swapping the order of words can change the joined word and its code.
limits.item1: The worked pair illustrates the law. The general argument depends on place value for every suffix length and on the digits giving each positive code a unique decoding.
limits.item2: The catalog export analogy concerns resolved links. An export that aims to reconstruct full catalog records also needs to preserve unresolved titles, definitions and provenance.

steps.wordsFirst: Start with L followed by R. Join the words by putting R after L.
steps.encodeJoinedWord: LR gives the digits 12 in base three, which represent 5.
steps.codesFirst: Start again with the same pair. This time encode L and R separately.
steps.combineSeparateCodes: Shift 1 by one base-three place and add 2. Both routes meet at 5.
steps.recoverTheWord: Read the digits 12 from left to right and turn them back into L and R.
steps.outsideTheImage: In base three, 3 is written 10. The digit 0 has no letter, so this positive number lies outside the image.

model.caption: Words are on the left and their codes on the right. Both routes reach 5. The return arrow and the detached candidate show where decoding works.

intuition.text: A Gödel number gives a piece of written syntax an integer that can be read back. The payoff is that what you do with the writing can now have a counterpart in arithmetic. Here you can join L and R by writing one after the other, or by doing arithmetic on their two codes. In Gödel’s proof, a coding of formal syntax lets arithmetic describe expressions and derivations, including those written in the language of arithmetic itself.
intuition.situation: DotLn-Angular’s public Toolbox catalog document offers an analogy. A mapped concept’s ID keeps the map slug and the original line number. Given the map, a machine can use that address to find a source row. This exercise goes one step further by storing the letters themselves in an integer and recovering them by division.

example.name: Encode L followed by R
example.description: We assigned L the digit 1 and R the digit 2. Joining L and R writes 12 in base three, or 1 × 3 + 2 = 5. To read 5 back, divide it by 3. The quotient is 1 and the remainder 2 gives R. Divide 1 by 3. The quotient is 0 and the remainder 1 gives L. Reverse that order to recover LR. The set of numbers the encoder can produce is its image. Try candidate 3 to find why some integers are outside it.

step0.title: Accumulate the digits
step0.text: Start at zero. For each letter, multiply the current code by three and add its digit. Encode L and R separately. Also encode the word LR so you have both routes to compare.

step1.title: Join the numbers
step1.text: Count the base-three places in R’s code. For the empty word, count zero places. Multiply L’s code by that power of three and add R’s code. The result has the same digits, in the same order, as the encoding of LR.

step2.title: Recover the letters
step2.text: Divide the joined code by three and save the remainder. Keep dividing the quotient until it reaches zero. The remainders give the letters rightmost first, so reverse their order to get LR.

step3.title: Test the candidate
step3.text: Zero codes the empty word. A negative number or a positive numeral containing a zero digit falls outside the image. All other base-three numerals use only the digits 1 and 2 and decode to a unique word.

pseudocode.ordinary:
digit = { L: 1, R: 2 }
encode(word):
  code = 0
  for symbol in word:
    code = code × 3 + digit[symbol]
  return code
leftCode = encode(leftWord)  // L
rightCode = encode(rightWord)  // R
codeFromWords = encode(concatenate(leftWord, rightWord))  // LR

places = length of rightCode in base three (0 when rightCode = 0)
codeFromNumbers = leftCode × 3^places + rightCode
check codeFromNumbers = codeFromWords

decode(code):
  if code < 0: reject
  letters = []
  while code > 0:
    quotient, remainder = divide code by 3
    if remainder = 0: reject
    add the letter for remainder to letters
    code = quotient
  return reverse(letters)
recovered = decode(codeFromNumbers)  // LR

try decode(probeCode)
  accepted word → inside the image
  rejected code → outside the image

item0.relevance: A worked prime-power coding of formal expressions.
item0.explanation: Panu Raatikainen gives each primitive symbol a number and uses the powers of successive primes to hold those symbol numbers in order. Factoring a code recovers the exponents. The supplement then shows how checking formula shape and forming a negation can be stated in terms of codes. This study uses base-three place value for its smaller alphabet.

item2.title: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

item0.why: See why the two routes agree for every pair of words and which set the inverse covers.

item1.why: Joining codes by shifting and adding gives a concrete example of turning a typographical operation into arithmetic.

item2.why: The Gödel sentence uses a numbering of formal syntax together with diagonalization to express a claim about its provability.

limits.item0: This alphabet has letters and concatenation. To ask whether a word is a well-formed formula or whether a sequence proves it, an arithmetization also needs the formal grammar, the coding of derivations and the proof rules.
limits.item1: The image depends on this alphabet and number base. Another assignment of digits changes the code for a given word, and using zero for a letter would require a way to preserve leading zeros.
limits.item2: The catalog address needs the source map to recover the row. Its separate SHA-256 checks the source bytes. Recovering a word directly from its number requires the inverse used here.

step.encode: Start each code at zero. Multiply by three and add the digit for each letter in order.
step.joinCodes: The number of base-three places on the right is {{ rightPlaces }}. The join is {{ left }} × {{ multiplier }} + {{ right }} = {{ code }}.
step.joinWords: Write the second word after the first to see the same join on the word side.
step.compare: Encoding the joined word gives {{ codeFromWords }}. Joining the codes gives {{ codeFromNumbers }}.
step.decode: Repeatedly divide {{ code }} by three. Read the remainders in reverse order to recover {{ word }}.
step.probeWord: The candidate decodes to {{ word }} and belongs to the image.
step.probeNegative: Negative numbers are outside the image. The encoder starts at zero and appends positive digits.
step.probeZeroDigit: The numeral {{ ternary }} in base three has a zero digit. Dividing {{ dividend }} by three exposes that remainder, so the candidate is outside the image.

model.caption: The left side joins words. The right side makes the same join through arithmetic. Follow the return arrow to recover the joined word, then try the candidate.

intuition.text: A proof checker can tell you whether a particular list of lines makes a valid proof. In Peano arithmetic (PA), numbers can represent those lines and the whole proof. That lets PA express a claim about its own proofs. For the sentence G, the claim is that there is no number coding a PA proof of G itself.
intuition.situation: This is an analogy to DotLn’s public execution guide, which ties a passing review gate row to the code it checked. Say a work order for a link checker asks whether its test suite could pass even when the checker accepts a broken URL. A passing row gives the result for the code the suite ran against. To answer the work order’s question you have to ask what cases the suite can check and what counts as a pass.

example.name: G in Peano arithmetic
example.description: Hofstadter builds G in his Typographical Number Theory (TNT). Here is an adaptation in Peano arithmetic (PA). Its equality axiom gives a one-line proof of 0 = 0. Call the number encoding that proof p, and the number encoding its last formula n. The proof checker accepts the pair (p, n). Use this same numbering to build G and ask whether PA could prove it.

step0.title: Encode a PA proof
step0.text: Assign each formula and finite sequence of formulas its own code. A proof of 0 = 0 gives one number for the derivation and another for its conclusion. The arithmetic predicate Proof_PA checks whether a proposed pair of numbers encodes a valid PA proof of that conclusion.

step1.title: Leave one place to fill
step1.text: Define diagonalCode(x) by reading x as a formula with one free variable, filling that place with the numeral for x, and numbering the result. Make a formula B(x) saying that there is no PA proof whose conclusion has code diagonalCode(x).

step2.title: Plug in B’s own code
step2.text: Put the numeral for B’s code into B(x) to get G. By construction, diagonalCode applied to B’s code is the code of G. PA can verify this substitution and prove that G is equivalent to the statement that no code gives a PA proof of G.

step3.title: Suppose PA proves G
step3.text: The proof would supply a specific number, and PA could verify the number and prove that a proof of G exists. By the equivalence, PA would also prove that none exists. A consistent PA cannot prove both claims, so under that assumption PA has no proof of G.

step4.title: Read G in the natural numbers
step4.text: The absence of a PA proof means there is no ordinary natural number that the proof predicate accepts as a proof of G. With the standard encoding, that makes the arithmetic sentence G true in the ordinary natural numbers. The argument used PA’s consistency as a premise about PA.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: the sketch follows the proof about PA using its consistency as a premise.
theory = PeanoArithmetic
p = code(a derivation of "0 = 0" in theory)
n = code("0 = 0")
Proof_PA(p, n) holds

diagonalCode(x) = code(substituteNumeral(formulaWithCode(x), x))
B(x) means no p satisfies Proof_PA(p, diagonalCode(x))

b = code(B)
G = substituteNumeral(B, b)
PA proves G ↔ ¬∃p Proof_PA(p, numeral(code(G)))

assume PA is consistent
if a PA proof of G has code p:
    PA proves ∃q Proof_PA(q, numeral(code(G))) using numeral(p)
    PA proves ¬∃q Proof_PA(q, numeral(code(G))) using G
    contradiction

conclude there is no PA proof of G
in the natural numbers, no proof number exists, so G is true there

limits.item0: The argument from consistency excludes a PA proof of this G. Excluding a PA proof of its negation for this construction uses a stronger assumption, such as ω-consistency. That assumption rules out proving an existential claim while refuting every individual natural-number instance.
limits.item1: The proof predicate names a particular theory. Add G as an axiom and it has an immediate proof in the extended theory. The old G still concerns proofs in PA.
limits.item2: The gate analogy is about the scope of evidence. Engineers can read or extend a finite set of test cases. The arithmetic argument concerns all possible proof codes for a sentence constructed using the theory’s own proof predicate.

steps.encode-proof: Check the code of a derivation against the code of its last line, 0 = 0.
steps.make-template: B is a sentence template with one empty slot, x. Its claim concerns the sentence obtained by inserting the numeral for x into the template whose code is x. The function diagonalCode names that substitution.
steps.close-template: Insert the numeral for B’s own code. The conclusion named in the proof predicate now has the code of G.
steps.assume-consistency: A proof of G would let PA prove that such a proof both exists and does not exist.
steps.read-truth: If PA is consistent, no natural number codes a PA proof of G. With the standard encoding, G is true in the natural numbers.

model.caption: Follow the numeric codes from a PA proof to a sentence about PA’s own proofs. The last two arrows distinguish the absence of a proof in PA from truth in the natural numbers.

intuition.text: In a puzzle you can ask which move comes next, or you can ask what every allowed move has in common. The second question is about the rules themselves. If you find a property that survives every move, you can use it to tell whether a target is out of reach.
intuition.situation: This is an analogy to the recovery modes in DotLn’s public CLAUDE.md. That file describes analysis: as a pause for diagnosis, even when the repository or harness has failed, and gives analysis: off as the way to leave the mode. Imagine using that pause after a repeated gate failure to examine the gate’s setup. You can then resume the original workflow with a specific diagnosis to test.

example.name: Can MI reach MU?
example.description: Start with MI in the MIU puzzle and try to reach MU. A sequence of legal rewrites reaches MIU. To find out whether it is possible to finish with MU, count the I symbols and track the remainder after division by 3.

step0.title: Try a legal path
step0.text: Start from MI. Duplicate everything after M to produce MII. Do that again to make MIIII. Replace the last three I symbols with U to get MIU.

step1.title: Change what you track
step1.text: Track the number of I symbols modulo 3, the remainder when you divide by 3. The path MI, MII, MIIII, MIU has remainders 1, 2, 1, 1. Ask whether any legal step could take a nonzero remainder to zero.

step2.title: Check all the rules
step2.text: In the MIU rules, append U only after a word ending in I, or erase an adjacent UU. Either move keeps the I count. Replacing III by U subtracts three. Duplicating the tail (everything after M) doubles the count and swaps remainders 1 and 2. A nonzero remainder stays nonzero under every legal move. This preserved property is the invariant.

step3.title: Return to MU
step3.text: MU contains zero I symbols, so its remainder is zero. That excludes MU from every path starting at MI. The question now has an answer for paths of any length.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: one trial path leads to a written argument about every legal rewrite.
start = "MI"
target = "MU"
MII = duplicateTail(start)
MIIII = duplicateTail(MII)
MIU = replaceTrailingIIIWithU(MIIII)

modulus = 3
remainder(s) = count("I", s) mod modulus
observe remainders along [start, MII, MIIII, MIU] are [1, 2, 1, 1]

for r in [1, 2]:
    show (2 × r) mod modulus is 1 or 2  // duplicate the tail
    show (r − 3) mod modulus equals r  // replace III with U
// Appending U and removing UU both leave r unchanged.
conclude that all strings reached from start have a nonzero remainder

remainder(target) = 0
conclude that no legal path from start reaches target

item0.relevance: See the puzzle’s legal rewrites encoded as a proof checker’s rules.
item0.explanation: The Metamath database introduces MI as an axiom and represents each of the four rewrites as an inference. It ends with a concrete derivation of MUIIU. The Metamath handbook’s Appendix D explains that answering the reachability question for MU takes a separate argument about those rules.

item1.relevance: See the same structure in a proof about a concurrent algorithm.
item1.explanation: Lamport’s notes work through a mutual exclusion example, where two processes must never enter a critical section together. The proof uses an invariant that holds initially and survives every allowed step. That invariant implies mutual exclusion for every state reached by the algorithm.

limits.item0: This remainder argument depends on the exact rewrite rules. Add a rule that removes one I and the reachable string MIU can immediately become MU.
limits.item1: A target with a nonzero remainder passes this particular check. The argument leaves the path to that target to be found.
limits.item2: The DotLn analogy covers the shift to a question about the rules and the return to the original work. A human directs recovery in DotLn. The puzzle’s conclusion follows by checking a fixed set of rewrites.

steps.try-rewrites: Duplicate the tail twice to reach MII and then MIIII. Replace the last three I symbols with U to get MIU.
steps.count: Track the count of I symbols modulo 3. The remainders along the trial path are 1, 2, 1 and 1.
steps.check-rules: Two rules leave the count alone, one subtracts three, and doubling swaps remainders 1 and 2. Every rule preserves a nonzero remainder.
steps.rule-out-target: MU contains zero I symbols. Starting at MI gives remainder 1, so MU is unreachable from MI by these rules.

model.caption: Read up from the legal path to the property the rules preserve. The final arrow brings that property back to the target MU.

intuition.text: When an idea comes to mind, it can change which other ideas are easy to reach. In Hofstadter’s account, the role of an active symbol comes partly from what it brings into consideration. Think about what becomes relevant as soon as you intend to make tea.
intuition.situation: As a DotLn analogy, the public DotLn kit guide describes how entering resume: next directs a session to the executor’s skill through the generated operating contract. The phrase has that effect because the kit connects it to a procedure.

example.name: A kettle cues making tea
example.description: Imagine a kettle clicking off. The sound is the cue. The active symbol in this example is the idea of making tea that comes to mind. While it is active, it makes the ideas of a mug and a tea bag easier to recall. The two arrows trace these imagined associations. The mugs on the shelf stay where they are.

step0.title: Hear the kettle
step0.text: A click from the kettle switch supplies the cue.

step1.title: Think of making tea
step1.text: The familiar sound brings making tea to mind.

step2.title: Think of a mug
step2.text: A mug comes to mind as something to hold the tea.

step3.title: Think of a tea bag
step3.text: Another association from the same idea makes a tea bag relevant. The drawing follows each association separately so you can see that they share a source.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: this trace follows assumed associations in one kitchen.
cue = notice("Kettle click")
linksFromTea = ["Mug", "Tea bag"]

idea = activate("Making tea", cue)

consider(linksFromTea[0], from = idea)

consider(linksFromTea[1], from = idea)

item0.relevance: Concepts that change which other concepts a program considers.
item0.explanation: Copycat tries to transfer a change from one string of letters to another. Activation spreads among concepts in its Slipnet. The activation of opposite can also shorten the link between successor and predecessor, making it easier for the program to substitute one for the other when reading a string.

intuition.text: A clock revisits the same positions as time passes. A strange loop returns by changing the level at which you read something. In Escher’s Print Gallery, the room that holds a picture turns up inside what that picture depicts.

example.name: Back inside Escher’s Print Gallery
example.description: In M. C. Escher’s lithograph Print Gallery, find the visitor on the left looking at a print. Follow his gaze into its seaport. Trace the quayside buildings around to the gallery where that same visitor is standing. The gallery contains the print, and the city in the print contains the gallery. The map below lets you retrace that route. Escher left a white area in the center. The smaller rotated copy shown by the mathematical reconstruction belongs to that later work.

step0.title: Begin in the gallery
step0.text: Take the visitor’s room as your starting point.

step1.title: Look at the seaport print
step1.text: From the gallery, pick out the print as an object displayed on the wall.

step2.title: Read the seaport scene
step2.text: Follow what the seaport print depicts and look at the buildings along the waterfront.

step3.title: Recognize the gallery
step3.text: One of the buildings in the seaport scene is the same gallery where the print hangs.

step4.title: Return to the starting point
step4.text: Focus on the gallery again. It contains the print at one level and is part of the world depicted by the print at another.

pseudocode.ordinary:
// Illustrative: these steps record how to read the composition.
start = Gallery

print = Seaport print exhibited in start

scene = Seaport scene depicted by print

returnTo = Gallery as depicted within scene

focus(Gallery)
confirm returnTo represents start

specimen.title: Where does each instruction send you?
specimen.source: We wrote these two cards for this lesson. Imagine picking up the first card, doing what it says and putting it down. Then read the second.
specimen.reading: Both cards start the same way. Your eyes pick out the marks, then you read them as an instruction. Look at the last words on each card to decide what to count.
specimen.question: Which card sends you back to its own ink?
specimen.answer: The first sends your eyes to the room’s windows. The second sends them back to the letters that carry its own instruction. Its six words contain 25 letters. That return across levels is the loop.
